habitat: Green mambas inhabit the coastal forests, dense woodlands, and thickets of eastern and southern Africa, from Kenya south through Tanzania, Mozambique, and eastern Zimbabwe to South Africa's KwaZulu-Natal province. They are highly arboreal, spending most of their lives in trees, shrubs, and dense vegetation where their brilliant green coloration provides superb camouflage. They are seldom encountered on the ground unless crossing between trees or searching for prey. Deforestation and habitat fragmentation are shrinking their range.
diet: Green mambas are active, diurnal hunters that prey primarily on birds, bird eggs, bats, lizards, frogs, and small arboreal mammals. They use their exceptional eyesight to locate prey, then strike rapidly with potent neurotoxic venom delivered through fixed front fangs. Unlike the more aggressive black mamba, green mambas are shy and reluctant to bite, preferring to flee into dense vegetation when threatened. They typically hold onto prey until the venom takes effect, then swallow it whole.
behavior: Green mambas are nervous, alert snakes that rarely interact with humans unless cornered. When threatened, they may gape their mouth to display the striking blue-black interior — a warning display — before fleeing. They are solitary outside of mating season. Females lay 6-18 eggs in tree hollows, leaf litter, or rotting vegetation, which hatch after 10-12 weeks. Despite their venomous nature, they are preyed upon by birds of prey, mongooses, and other snakes. They are remarkably agile in trees, capable of moving rapidly through branches.
facts: Green mambas are among the most beautifully colored venomous snakes, with scales ranging from bright emerald to yellowish-green. Their venom is primarily neurotoxic, causing rapid paralysis, but bites to humans are extremely rare due to their shy nature and arboreal habitat. They reach lengths of 1.8-2.5 meters, smaller than their famous cousin the black mamba. Green mambas lack the black mouth lining of the black mamba — theirs is bluish-white. They can live up to 14 years in captivity.
naming: Green mamba names might reflect their brilliant coloration, arboreal nature, or African origin. Consider names like Emerald, Jade, Viper, Canopy, Slither, Verde, Basil, Kiwi, Forest, Lime, Mamba, Ivy, Amazon (for the rainforest association), or Vert (green in French).
